```{r message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
```

# Problem 1

```{r}
set.seed(1236)
birthday_repeated = function(n_room) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n_room, replace = TRUE)
  repeated_birthdays  = length(unique(birthdays)) < n_room
  return(repeated_birthdays)
}

birthday_repeated(147)
```

TRUE statement confirms that there are duplicate birthdays in the group.

```{r}
birthday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    number_of_people = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(number_of_people, birthday_repeated))
    
birthday_results_df |> 
  group_by(number_of_people) |> 
  summarize(prob_of_repeat = mean(repeated)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = number_of_people, y = prob_of_repeat)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Sharing Birthdays vs. Number of People in Room",
    x = "Number of People in Room",
    y = "Probability of Sharing Birthdays"
  )
```

Plot confirms that the probability of least two people in a group/room sharing a birthday increases when there is more people in the room. When this probability is 50%, there are about 22-23 people in the room.

# Problem 2

```{r}
study_df = 
  tibble(
    files = list.files("./data"), 
    path = str_c("./data/", files)
  ) |>
  mutate(data = purrr::map(path, read_csv, show_col_types= FALSE)) |> 
  unnest(data)
```

### Tidy Dataframe

```{r}
tidy_df = 
  study_df |> 
  mutate(
    files = str_replace(files, ".csv", ""),
    group = str_sub(files, 1, 3),
    group = case_match(
      group,
      "con" ~ "Control Arm",
      "exp" ~ "Experimental Arm"),
    subject_id = str_sub(files, 5, 6)) |> 
  pivot_longer(
    week_1:week_8,
    names_to = "week", 
    names_prefix = "week_", 
    values_to = "outcome") |>
  mutate(week = as.numeric(week)) |> 
    select(group, subject_id, subj = files, week, outcome)

tidy_df |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = outcome, group = subj, color = group)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(~group) + 
  labs(
    title = "Outcome of Subject vs. Week",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome of Subject",
    color = "Study Arm"
  )
```

Plot indicates while participants in the control arm seemed to have similar outcomes over the week (ranging from about -1.2 to 3.7), participants in the experimental arm had increased outcomes, scaling up from 0 to 7.5 over the week.

# Problem 3

```{r}
sim_ttest = function(mu){
  sim_data = 
    tibble(
      x = rnorm(30, mean = mu, sd = 5)
    )
  t.test(pull(sim_data, x), mu = 0) |> 
    broom::tidy() |> 
    select(estimate, p.value)}

set.seed(1236)

sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000) |> 
  mutate(
    est_df = map(mu, sim_ttest)) |> 
  unnest(est_df) |> 
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05)

sim_results_df
```

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(power = mean(rejected)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Power vs. True Population Mean",
    x = "True Population Mean",
    y = "Probability of Rejecting False Null Hypothesis (Power)"
  )
```

As the true population mean moves further away from the null, effect size increases, and power increases in a sigmoidal manner. This plot supports that power increases with effect size, meaning that studies with small true effect sizes may be underpowered compared to studies with larger true effect sizes. 

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(emp_mean = mean(estimate)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = emp_mean)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Average Mean Sample Estimate vs. True Population Mean",
    x = "True Population Mean",
    y = "Average Mean Sample Estimate"
  )
```

The relationship between average mean sample estimate and the true population mean follows a linear positive relationship where slope = 1. For every point on the graph, x=y across all values (Ex. (0,0), (1,1), (2,2), (3,3)...). This indicates that the sample mean is an unbiased estimator of the true population mean across multiple iterations. 

```{r}
sim_results_df |> 
  filter(rejected == TRUE) |> 
  group_by(mu) |> 
  summarize(
    emp_mean = mean(estimate)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = emp_mean)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_line() + 
  labs(
    title = "Average Mean Sample Estimate Where Null Rejected vs. True Population Mean",
    x = "True Population Mean",
    y = "Average Mean Sample Estimate Where Null Rejected"
  )
```

After filtering by samples for which the null was rejected, we found that the average mean estimate overestimated the true population mean at smaller effect sizes (x = 1, 2, and 3). This shows how lower power may lead to less accurate estimates when detecting true effect sizes. At higher effect sizes, average sample estimate was more indicative of the true population mean due to higher power.
